questions.stem: Which task is a main purpose of an asset pricing model?

options.A: To calculate a fund's management expense ratio
options.B: To set the discount rate used to value a security
options.C: To measure the largest fall from a peak to a later low
options.D: To set the client's time horizon and liquidity needs

questions.rationale: An asset pricing model estimates the return that investors require for an asset's risk. Managers use that return as a discount rate, to judge fair price and to test alpha. Time horizon and liquidity come from the client's KYC information. Drawdown is a risk measure.

questions.stem: Why does the CAPM give a reward only for systematic risk?

options.A: Systematic risk is always larger than unsystematic risk
options.B: Standard deviation cannot measure unsystematic risk
options.C: Investors can remove unsystematic risk by diversification at no cost
options.D: Regulators require models to ignore company-specific risk

questions.rationale: In the CAPM, diversification removes unsystematic risk at no cost, so the market pays no premium for it. Only beta, the exposure to market risk, earns a reward. The relative size of the two risks is not the reason.

questions.stem: Which statement describes a disadvantage of the CAPM?

options.A: The true market portfolio that it needs cannot be observed
options.B: It does not say which factors or how many factors to use
options.C: It needs data on size, value, profitability and investment
options.D: It rewards unsystematic risk that diversification can remove

questions.rationale: The CAPM needs the true market portfolio, which no one can observe. Its other weaknesses are unrealistic assumptions and a single beta that often explains returns poorly. The failure to name the factors is a weakness of the APT, not of the CAPM.

questions.stem: Gisela Castellano prefers arbitrage pricing theory (APT) to the CAPM, because the APT needs fewer assumptions. Which drawback of the APT must she accept?

options.A: The theory needs the true market portfolio, which no one can observe
options.B: The theory does not name the factors or say how many to use
options.C: The theory allows only one factor, which is beta to the market
options.D: The theory adds momentum, which is volatile and costly to trade

questions.rationale: The APT explains return with several systematic factors but does not name them or their number. So the choice of factors is subjective. An unobservable market portfolio is a CAPM weakness. Costly momentum trading is a weakness of the Carhart model.

questions.stem: Two well-diversified portfolios have the same exposures to inflation, GDP growth and interest rates. Under arbitrage pricing theory, what must be true?

options.A: The portfolio with more holdings must have the higher expected return
options.B: Their expected returns can differ because of their unsystematic risk
options.C: The portfolio with the lower price must have the lower expected return
options.D: They must have the same expected return

questions.rationale: The APT rests on no-arbitrage. Portfolios with the same factor exposures must have the same expected return. Otherwise, traders could buy one, sell the other and earn a riskless profit. Unsystematic risk earns no extra return.

questions.stem: Which factor is in the Fama–French five-factor model but not in the Carhart four-factor model?

options.A: Momentum (winners minus losers)
options.B: Profitability (robust minus weak)
options.C: Value (high minus low)
options.D: Size (small minus big)

questions.rationale: Carhart uses the market, size and value factors plus momentum. The Fama–French five-factor model uses market, size and value plus profitability and investment. So profitability is only in the five-factor model. Momentum is only in Carhart, and size and value are in both.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 6.7 multi-factor table and exam trap

questions.stem: A researcher adds a momentum factor to the Fama–French five-factor model. Which statement about the new model is correct?

options.A: It has four factors and is the same as the Carhart model
options.B: It has six factors and is the simplest multi-factor model
options.C: It has five factors, because momentum replaces investment
options.D: It has six factors and the greatest risk of data-mining

questions.rationale: Five factors plus momentum give six factors. This model covers the most known anomalies, but it is the most complex and has the greatest risk of data-mining. The Carhart model has four factors: the three original Fama–French factors plus momentum.

questions.stem: In a multi-factor model, what does the value factor (HML) measure?

options.A: Returns of high book-to-market stocks minus low book-to-market stocks
options.B: Returns of firms with robust profitability minus firms with weak profitability
options.C: Returns of stocks with high recent returns minus those with low recent returns
options.D: Returns of large companies minus returns of small companies

questions.rationale: HML means high minus low book-to-market, so it compares cheap (value) stocks with expensive ones. Winners minus losers is the momentum factor. Robust minus weak profitability is RMW. The size factor is small minus big, not large minus small.

questions.stem: Use a T-bill yield of 3.5% and a market risk premium of 6%. Shares of Norlake Corp. have a beta of 1.25. What return does the CAPM require for them?
questions.rationale: Required return = 3.5% + 1.25 × 6% = 11.0%. The premium is already given, so do not subtract the risk-free rate again. The 7.5% result omits the risk-free rate. The 9.5% result ignores beta.

questions.stem: Vasco Lombardi's analyst forecasts an 11.5% return for a stock with a beta of 1.6. T-bills yield 2%, and the market should return 7%. What should Vasco conclude?

options.A: Alpha is −1.5%, so the stock is overvalued
options.B: Alpha is −1.7%, so the stock is overvalued
options.C: Alpha is +1.5%, so the stock is undervalued
options.D: Alpha is +0.3%, so the stock is fairly priced

questions.rationale: The CAPM return is 2% + 1.6 × (7% − 2%) = 10.0%. The forecast is 1.5% higher, so the stock plots above the SML and is undervalued. The +0.3% result multiplies beta by the market return, not by the premium.

questions.stem: Tavish Vandermeer splits his money: 30% in a stock (beta 1.4), 50% in an equity fund (beta 1.0) and 20% in T-bills. What is his portfolio's beta?
questions.rationale: Portfolio beta is the weighted average: 0.3 × 1.4 + 0.5 × 1.0 + 0.2 × 0 = 0.92. T-bills have a beta of zero but still count in the weights. The 0.80 result is a simple average, and 1.15 leaves the T-bills out.

questions.stem: An analyst says that a stock must return 12% to compensate for its risk under the CAPM. T-bills yield 3%, and the market should return 9%. What beta does this imply?
questions.rationale: Solve 12% = 3% + β × (9% − 3%). So β = 9% ÷ 6% = 1.50. The 1.33 result divides 12% by the market return. The 1.00 result divides the 9% excess return by the market return instead of by the premium.

questions.stem: Yannick Abelard wants a CAPM expected return of 7%. He will mix a market index fund (beta 1.0) with T-bills. T-bills yield 3%, and the market should return 8%. What weight goes in the index fund?
questions.rationale: He needs a beta of (7% − 3%) ÷ (8% − 3%) = 0.80. The index fund has a beta of 1.0 and T-bills have a beta of zero, so 80% goes in the fund. The 87.5% result divides 7% by 8%. The 20% result is the T-bill weight.

questions.stem: Ulla Ferreiro wants a higher CAPM expected return for her portfolio. The risk-free rate and the expected market return stay the same. What must she accept?

options.A: A higher portfolio beta, which means more market risk
options.B: A higher standard deviation with the same beta
options.C: A larger share of T-bills in her portfolio
options.D: More unsystematic risk from fewer holdings

questions.rationale: In the CAPM, expected return rises only with beta, so she must accept more market risk. The CAPM pays nothing for unsystematic risk or for volatility that does not come from beta. More T-bills lower beta and so lower the expected return.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 6.8 expected return and risk of a portfolio

questions.stem: T-bills yield 3%, and the market should return 8%. Stock X has a standard deviation of 45% and a beta of 0.4. Stock Y has a standard deviation of 20% and a beta of 1.3. Which stock has the higher CAPM required return?

options.A: Stock Y, because a lower standard deviation always earns more
options.B: Neither, because both must return only the 3% risk-free rate
options.C: Stock X, because the CAPM rewards its higher standard deviation
options.D: Stock Y, at 9.5%, because the CAPM prices only beta

questions.rationale: Stock X requires 3% + 0.4 × 5% = 5.0%. Stock Y requires 3% + 1.3 × 5% = 9.5%. The CAPM rewards only systematic risk, which beta measures. Most of Stock X's high volatility is unsystematic, and diversification can remove it.

questions.stem: T-bills yield 4%, and the market should return 9%. Which stock below is undervalued under the CAPM?

options.A: Stock S: beta 1.0, forecast return 8.5%
options.B: Stock R: beta 1.5, forecast return 11.0%
options.C: Stock Q: beta 0.6, forecast return 8.0%
options.D: Stock P: beta 1.2, forecast return 10.0%

questions.rationale: Required returns are 4% + β × 5%: P 10.0%, Q 7.0%, R 11.5% and S 9.0%. Only Stock Q has a forecast above its required return, so it plots above the SML. Stock P plots on the SML. Stocks R and S plot below it.
questions.qa_note: calc: required = 4 + b x 5 -> P 10.0 (fcst 10.0), Q 7.0 (fcst 8.0), R 11.5 (fcst 11.0), S 9.0 (fcst 8.5)

questions.stem: Bronwen Tallis puts half her money in an index fund (beta 1.0), 30% in a stock (beta 1.6) and the rest in T-bills. T-bills yield 2.5%, and the market should return 8.5%. What is her CAPM expected return?
questions.rationale: Portfolio beta = 0.5 × 1.0 + 0.3 × 1.6 + 0.2 × 0 = 0.98. Expected return = 2.5% + 0.98 × 6% = 8.38%. The 5.88% result omits the risk-free rate. The 10.83% result multiplies beta by the market return, not by the premium.

questions.stem: Under weak-form efficiency, which information do market prices already reflect?

options.A: All past price and volume data
options.B: All public information, including financial statements
options.C: All information, both public and private
options.D: Only the information in company press releases

questions.rationale: Weak-form efficiency means that prices reflect all past price and volume data, so technical analysis cannot earn abnormal returns. The semi-strong form adds all public information. The strong form adds private information too.

questions.stem: Suppose a market is strong-form efficient. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Only insider information can give consistent abnormal returns
options.B: Only fundamental analysis of public data can give abnormal returns
options.C: Technical analysis can give abnormal returns, but fundamental analysis cannot
options.D: Not even insider information can give consistent abnormal returns

questions.rationale: Strong-form prices reflect all information, public and private, so no information gives an edge. Insider information gives an edge only if the market is semi-strong but not strong-form efficient. The strong form includes the weaker forms, so technical and fundamental analysis also fail.

questions.stem: Henrik Brannock buys software that finds buy signals in past stock prices and trading volume. The market is weak-form efficient. What should he expect?

options.A: Lower risk, because the signals avoid all market declines
options.B: No abnormal returns, but lower costs than an index fund
options.C: Consistent abnormal returns, because the software is faster than analysts
options.D: No consistent abnormal returns, and higher trading costs

questions.rationale: Weak-form efficiency means that prices already reflect past price and volume data. So signals from those data cannot give consistent abnormal returns. Each extra trade adds spreads and commissions, so his costs rise above those of a low-cost index fund.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 6.9 weak form; chart-pattern scenario

questions.stem: Petra Hargreaves believes that large Canadian stocks are close to semi-strong efficient. Which approach best fits this belief for her core holdings?

options.A: A fund that rotates sectors on public economic forecasts
options.B: A fund that picks stocks from public financial statements
options.C: A low-cost fund that tracks a broad index
options.D: A fund that trades on chart patterns each week

questions.rationale: In a semi-strong efficient market, prices adjust quickly to all public information. Research on public data is then unlikely to earn more than its cost. So the EMH favours passive, low-cost indexing. The other funds rely on public data that prices already reflect.

questions.stem: Suppose markets are efficient. How can a portfolio manager still add value for a client?

options.A: By setting the asset mix and controlling costs and taxes
options.B: By moving to cash when chart signals show a peak
options.C: By buying the funds with the best returns last year
options.D: By picking stocks that look cheap in published reports

questions.rationale: If prices already reflect information, security selection is unlikely to beat its cost. The manager adds value in other ways: set the asset mix, manage risk, control costs and taxes, and fit the portfolio to the client. Published reports and charts are data that prices already reflect.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 6.9 implications for portfolio management

questions.stem: According to the EMH, why are future price changes hard to predict?

options.A: Prices change only on private information that the public never sees
options.B: New information arrives at random, and competing analysts quickly move prices to fair value
options.C: Most investors ignore news, so prices drift slowly toward fair value over time
options.D: Regulators stop analysts from trading on new public information until it is old

questions.rationale: The EMH rests on competition. Many analysts search for mispriced securities, and their trades quickly move prices to fair value. New information arrives at random, so the next price change is hard to predict. A slow drift would make prices predictable.

questions.stem: Where does the evidence suggest that active managers have the most room to add value?

options.A: In less-followed segments, such as small-cap stocks
options.B: In large stocks that many analysts follow closely
options.C: In markets that are strong-form efficient
options.D: In the stocks with the most daily news coverage

questions.rationale: Most observers see large, heavily followed markets as close to semi-strong efficient. Fewer analysts follow small caps and some bonds, so these segments may leave more room for active managers. In a strong-form efficient market, no information gives an edge.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 6.9 limits of the EMH

questions.stem: Yorick Haverford starts with a forecast of strong GDP growth. Next, he picks the sectors likely to gain most. Last, he picks companies in those sectors. Which weakness is most specific to his approach?

options.A: He can pay a premium for growth that later slows
options.B: He can overlook sector and economic risk in his holdings
options.C: He can buy cheap stocks whose businesses are in permanent decline
options.D: He can miss good companies in the sectors that he does not favour

questions.rationale: Economy first, then sectors, then companies is a top-down approach. Top-down captures macro and sector trends, but it can miss good companies in the wrong sectors. Overlooking sector or economic risk is the typical weakness of a bottom-up manager.

questions.stem: Winnie Sandoval picks 20 stocks only on company fundamentals and pays little attention to the economy. Later, 65% of her fund is in one sector. Which risk does this show?

options.A: Cap-weighted indexing concentrates in the largest companies
options.B: Market timing needs two correct forecasts to succeed
options.C: Bottom-up selection can overlook sector and economic risk
options.D: Top-down selection can miss good companies in weak sectors

questions.rationale: Winnie studies companies first, so she is a bottom-up manager. Bottom-up finds individual mispricings but can overlook sector or macro risk. Here her stock choices built a large sector bet that she did not plan. Missing good companies in weak sectors is the top-down weakness.

questions.stem: Rafferty Montague expects the economy to enter a contraction. He keeps his fund fully invested in equities but moves into consumer staples, utilities and health care. Which technique does he use?

options.A: Buy and hold
options.B: Market timing
options.C: Sector rotation
options.D: Value investing

questions.rationale: Rafferty overweights the sectors that he expects to lead in the next phase of the cycle, so he uses sector rotation. Defensive sectors fit a contraction. He is not a market timer, because he does not switch out of equities into cash or bonds.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 6.10 sector rotation vs market timing

questions.stem: Which list matches the common textbook pattern of sector rotation over the business cycle?

options.A: Early expansion: energy; late expansion: utilities; contraction: financials
options.B: Early expansion: utilities; late expansion: financials; contraction: energy
options.C: Early expansion: financials; late expansion: energy; contraction: utilities
options.D: Early expansion: financials; late expansion: utilities; contraction: energy

questions.rationale: In the textbook pattern, cyclicals such as consumer discretionary and financials lead in early expansion. Energy and materials lead in late expansion. Defensives such as staples, utilities and health care lead in contraction. Actual leadership varies from cycle to cycle.

questions.stem: Dov Szymanski buys a stock with a P/E ratio of 4 and a dividend yield of 9%. A new technology is replacing the company's main product. Which risk matters most here?

options.A: Growth risk: both earnings and a high P/E multiple can fall at the same time
options.B: Timing risk: he must be right about both the exit and the re-entry
options.C: A value trap: the stock is cheap because its business is in permanent decline
options.D: Tracking error: the stock can move differently from its benchmark index

questions.rationale: A low P/E and a high yield make this a value purchase. The main danger in value investing is a value trap, a stock that is cheap because its business is in permanent decline. A falling high P/E is a growth-stock risk, and this multiple is already low.

questions.stem: Which pair of traits is most typical of the stocks that a growth manager buys?

options.A: Low P/E ratios and high dividend yields
options.B: Low P/E ratios and low earnings growth
options.C: High P/E ratios and low dividend yields
options.D: Low price-to-book ratios and high dividend yields

questions.rationale: Growth managers buy companies with above-average earnings growth. Their prices already include that growth, so P/E ratios are high, and their dividends are often low. Low P/E, low price-to-book and high dividend yield are value traits.

questions.stem: Two managers act on the same forecast. Eulalie Drummond raises equities from 60% to 65%, inside her policy range. Umberto Quarles cuts equities from 80% to 20% and holds cash. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Both make tactical tilts, because both keep some equities
options.B: Umberto is a market timer, and Eulalie makes a tactical tilt
options.C: Both are market timers, because both act on a forecast
options.D: Eulalie is a market timer, and Umberto makes a tactical tilt

questions.rationale: Market timing is the extreme form of tactical allocation: large switches between equities and cash on market forecasts. A tactical tilt is a smaller move inside set ranges around the strategic mix. Both moves use a forecast, so the size and the range decide the label.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 6.10 market timing vs tactical allocation

questions.stem: Xiomara Underhill moved her equities to cash before a market fall. She will wait for clear signs of recovery before she buys again. Why can this cost her much of her long-run return?

options.A: She can miss a few very strong days, which give a large part of long-run returns
options.B: Recoveries are always slower than the falls that come before them
options.C: Cash always loses value faster than equities lose value during a market fall
options.D: Equities pay no dividends during a recovery, so she loses no income by waiting

questions.rationale: Out of the market, a timer can miss a few very strong days, and those days give a large part of long-run returns. If she waits for clear signs of recovery, she can be in cash on those days. This risk adds to the risk of a wrong exit.

questions.stem: Valka Prentice says: "I am a value manager, so I must use a bottom-up process." Which reply is correct?

options.A: Incorrect: value is a style, which a manager can run top-down or bottom-up
options.B: Incorrect: value managers must always start with an economic forecast
options.C: Correct: value managers must study company ratios before the economy
options.D: Correct: only growth managers can use a top-down process

questions.rationale: Growth and value are styles. Top-down and bottom-up describe the order of analysis. A manager can combine either style with either approach. So a value manager can choose favoured sectors first and then buy the cheapest companies in them.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes a buy-and-hold portfolio from an index portfolio?

options.A: The buy-and-hold portfolio has high turnover; the index portfolio has none
options.B: The buy-and-hold manager chose the securities; the index manager copies a benchmark
options.C: The buy-and-hold manager rebalances to targets; the index manager never trades
options.D: The buy-and-hold portfolio has no market risk; the index portfolio has full market risk

questions.rationale: Both are passive and trade little. But a buy-and-hold manager still selected the original securities, while an index manager copies a benchmark such as the S&P/TSX Composite. A buy-and-hold manager does not rebalance, so the mix drifts. Both carry market risk.

questions.stem: Folasade Eriksen bought 12 stocks 18 years ago and never traded or rebalanced. One stock is now 35% of her portfolio. Which statement best describes her risk?

options.A: Her risk now equals the risk of a broad market index
options.B: Her risk has drifted into a large concentration in one issuer
options.C: Her risk is unchanged, because she still holds the same 12 stocks
options.D: Her risk is low, because buy and hold removes market risk

questions.rationale: Without rebalancing, a buy-and-hold mix drifts, so its risk changes over time. The best performer grew to 35%, which is an issuer concentration. The same names do not keep the same weights or risk. Buy and hold does not remove market risk.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 6.11 buy and hold drift

questions.stem: An index fund holds 140 of the 220 stocks in its index. The manager chose them as a representative subset and uses no optimization model. Which indexing method is this?

options.A: Optimization
options.B: Full replication
options.C: Sector rotation
options.D: Sampling

questions.rationale: Sampling holds a representative subset of the index. Full replication holds every index stock at its index weight. Optimization uses a model to minimize the deviation from the index. Sector rotation is an active technique, not an indexing method.

questions.stem: An index ETF trails its index by close to the same amount every year. Which cause best explains most of this tracking difference?

options.A: The timing of trades during the year
options.B: Cash drag that changes with fund flows
options.C: Sampling of the index stocks
options.D: The fund's fees

questions.rationale: Fees reduce the return by about the same amount each year, so they cause most of the tracking difference. Sampling, cash drag and trade timing have effects that change from period to period. They cause most of the tracking error.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 6.11 tracking difference vs tracking error

questions.stem: An index fund's return gap with its index swings between −0.6% and +0.5% from month to month. On average, the gap is small. Which cause best fits this pattern?

options.A: The fund holds only a sample of the index stocks
options.B: The fund carries full market risk, like its index
options.C: The fund's index is weighted by market capitalization
options.D: The fund charges a fixed annual management fee

questions.rationale: A gap that changes a lot but is small on average shows high tracking error, not a large tracking difference. Sampling, cash drag and trade timing cause most tracking error. A steady fee mainly causes a steady tracking difference. Market risk affects the fund and the index alike.

questions.stem: Ansel Jankowski holds a cap-weighted Canadian equity index fund. He sees that a few sectors and the largest stocks make up much of the fund. Which disadvantage of indexing does this show?

options.A: Index funds carry security-selection risk from manager choices
options.B: Cap weighting concentrates the fund in the largest stocks and sectors
options.C: Full replication increases tracking error over time
options.D: Index funds have high turnover and poor tax efficiency

questions.rationale: A cap-weighted index gives the most weight to the largest companies, which are sometimes overvalued. So the fund can concentrate in a few stocks or sectors. Indexing has low turnover and good tax efficiency, and it largely removes security-selection risk.

questions.stem: Hedda Yamamoto wants an index fund that beats the S&P/TSX Composite in rising markets. Which reply is accurate?

options.A: The fund beats the index if it uses full replication
options.B: The fund beats the index in rising markets because its fees are low
options.C: The fund's return is capped at the index return less costs
options.D: The fund can beat the index whenever its tracking error is high

questions.rationale: Passive management accepts the market return and does not try to beat it. The index return less costs is the ceiling. Low fees narrow the gap but do not lift the fund above the index. High tracking error means less consistent tracking, not a reliable gain.

questions.stem: A bond manager expects interest rates to rise. Which step fits this forecast?

options.A: Move into long-term strip bonds
options.B: Set duration equal to the client's horizon
options.C: Lengthen the portfolio's duration
options.D: Shorten the portfolio's duration

questions.rationale: Bond prices fall when rates rise, and a longer duration means a larger price fall. So a manager who expects higher rates shortens duration. Long strip bonds lengthen duration. Matching duration to a horizon is immunization, a passive technique with no rate forecast.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 6.12 duration management and exam trap

questions.stem: A manager lengthens duration because she expects interest rates to fall. Instead, rates rise. What is the result?

options.A: Prices rise, because longer bonds pay higher coupons
options.B: Higher reinvestment income fully offsets the price loss
options.C: Nothing changes, because duration affects only cash flows
options.D: Prices fall more than they would have at the old duration

questions.rationale: Duration management gains if the rate forecast is right and loses more if it is wrong. With a longer duration, a rise in rates causes a larger price fall than at the old duration. A full offset from reinvestment income is the aim of immunization, not of a rate bet.

questions.stem: A manager sells a bond and buys a nearly identical bond that offers a slightly higher yield. Which technique is this?

options.A: A substitution swap
options.B: Immunization
options.C: A rate anticipation swap
options.D: An intermarket spread swap

questions.rationale: A substitution swap exchanges a bond for a near-identical bond at a better yield. A rate anticipation swap changes maturity or duration to match a rate forecast. An intermarket swap moves between sectors when a spread looks too wide or too narrow.

questions.stem: Mattias Fairweather sells a bond at a capital loss in a tax-loss swap. He wants similar exposure and a deductible loss. Which replacement fits?

options.A: The identical bond, bought 25 days before the sale and still held
options.B: The identical bond, bought by his spouse 10 days after the sale
options.C: The identical bond, bought back 20 days after the sale
options.D: A similar but not identical bond, bought right after the sale

questions.rationale: A tax-loss swap buys a similar, not identical, bond. The superficial loss rule denies the loss if he or an affiliated person buys identical property within 30 days before or after the sale. A spouse is an affiliated person.
questions.source_quote: "You, or a person affiliated with you, buys, or has a right to buy, the same or identical property" — research/sources/cra/capital-gains-losses-superficial-loss-pages.txt CRA superficial loss page, ~line 728
questions.qa_note: regulatory: guide 6.12 tax-loss swap; 7.9 conditions (affiliated incl. spouse)

questions.stem: A manager thinks that the yield spread between provincial and corporate bonds is too wide. She sells provincial bonds and buys corporate bonds. Which swap is this?

options.A: An intermarket (yield-spread) swap
options.B: A rate anticipation swap
options.C: A tax-loss swap
options.D: A substitution swap

questions.rationale: An intermarket swap moves between bond sectors when a spread looks too wide or too narrow. She expects the spread to narrow, so corporates should gain against provincials. A substitution swap uses a near-identical bond, and a rate anticipation swap acts on a rate forecast.

questions.stem: A bond index holds too many issues for a manager to buy them all. How does an index-matching manager usually build the portfolio?

options.A: Hold only the index's largest issues, whatever their duration
options.B: Hold a sample that matches the index's duration, sector and credit quality
options.C: Hold a ladder of bonds with staggered maturities to the horizon
options.D: Set the portfolio's duration equal to the client's horizon

questions.rationale: Index matching copies a bond index at low cost. The index holds too many issues, so the manager holds a sample that matches it in duration, sector and credit quality. The main risk is tracking error. A ladder is buy and hold, and horizon matching is immunization.

questions.stem: A portfolio is immunized for a five-year horizon. Interest rates then rise. What offsets the fall in bond prices?

options.A: A matching rise in the bonds' par values
options.B: Higher income from reinvesting coupons at the new rates
options.C: Higher prices on the longer bonds in the portfolio
options.D: A rise in the portfolio's credit quality

questions.rationale: Immunization sets the portfolio's Macaulay duration equal to the horizon. If rates rise, prices fall, but coupons are reinvested at higher rates. If rates fall, higher prices offset the lower reinvestment income. Par values do not change, and longer bonds fall most when rates rise.

questions.stem: Zelda Calloway holds a ladder of corporate bonds to maturity. She believes that she will get par back on every bond. Which risk can make her wrong?

options.A: Interest rate risk
options.B: Issuer (credit) risk
options.C: Reinvestment risk
options.D: Inflation risk

questions.rationale: Held to maturity, each bond repays par whatever the level of interest rates. Reinvestment risk affects the rate on the money that matures, and inflation affects its buying power. But if an issuer defaults, she does not get par back. A ladder keeps issuer risk.
questions.qa_note: concept: guide 6.12 buy and hold ladder
